1.note: Aramaic, literally "a tarkav (a measure of two kav) of dinars", a Talmudic idiom for a large sum of money. He probably means the money spent on the journey from Paris.

2.he: ור' אזיק ואשתו זכרו ממני מזה כ"ב שנה כשהייתי שם
2.note: The place is not named; it is somewhere on the road from Flanders to Amsterdam. Twenty-two years earlier (about 1756) he was in Holland on his first mission.

3.note: The words of Exod 1:19 ("for they are lively"), printed with abbreviation marks (חיו"ת), as if an acronym or a play on words is meant. The sense here is not clear; translated literally.

4.note: A vehicle; the word occurs several times in this part. Perhaps from Spanish or Portuguese silla ("chair"), that is a sedan chair, or the horse-drawn sledge-carriage (Dutch slee, sleekoets) used in the streets of Amsterdam in these years. Translated "carriage" throughout.

5.note: Literally "seven blessings", the blessings of the wedding ceremony. What follows is a wedding: the blessing of betrothal and the seven blessings are the "eight blessings" said under the canopy.

6.note: פרכים is not a known word; from the context, a gesture of respect or courtesy. Perhaps a misprint.

7.note: Unclear: "he passed right in front of me, from behind him" (perhaps behind the bridegroom or the cantor). Translated literally.

8.note: Read as חולה, "ill" (he went because Teixeira de Mattos was ill). It could also be read חול, "a weekday".

9.note: Italian or Spanish presidente: the president of the wardens (the Mahamad) of the Portuguese community, to whom the emissary presented his letter of appointment.

10.note: Probably Spanish or Portuguese pan esponjado / pão espongado, "sponge bread", a sponge cake (compare the pan di Spagna in part 5).

11.note: Printed עז"ת סופר; A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34), p. 138, reads עזרת סופר, Ezrat Sofer ("the scribe's help"). GPT proposes Judah Piza's five-volume Amsterdam Pentateuch of that title (Janson and Mondovy, 1767–69); not checked.

12.note: Read as a name, Signor Ḥada (or Hadda). It could also mean "to a certain Signor" (Aramaic ḥada, "one"); not certain.

13.note: החה"ש read as החכם השלם, "the perfect sage" (a common title), and שד"ר as sheliaḥ de-rabbanan, "the emissary": the Ḥida himself.

14.note: רוחים read as ריוחים, "gains, values": the fall of the stocks in London. In March 1778 France announced its treaty with the American colonies, and British funds fell; this is probably the crash he means.

15.note: "That I had not visited him": the person is not named, perhaps Aaron Capadose, mentioned just before.

16.he: החכם יצחק בן דאנא די בריטו
16.note: Probably Isaac Ḥayyim Abendana de Brito, ḥakham (chief rabbi) of the Portuguese community of Amsterdam, who died in 1760. Solomon Shalem succeeded him. The "Signor ben Dana" of paragraph 81 is another, living member of the family.

17.note: Read as חלקתיה, "which I distributed": the printed letter of the mission that the emissary handed out. Not certain.

18.note: So printed: Purim (14 Adar) had been eight days earlier, on 13 March. The text gives no reason for the late celebration.

19.note: A gentile named Britano (Brittano?), not identified. The print separates it from "ben Dana" with a full stop; it is perhaps possible that it belongs to his name (de Brito), but then only two gentiles would be listed.

20.note: A Dutch name, read as Ebelsman (or Ibelsman); not identified.

21.note: A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34), p. 140, reads קארלו בירנאנדי, Carlo Birnandi, and spells the great merchant of part 7 (printed וידאנאנדי) almost the same way (p. 145): very probably one man, a gentile merchant of Amsterdam. The European spelling of the name is not known.
